splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in the defendant's favor. This split affects how sentencing enhancements are applied in thousands of federal criminal cases and implicates fundamental questions about the scope of agency power in criminal contexts after Loper Bright.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, because delegated power should not be used to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary prevails over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference after Kisor v. Wilkie when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1's expansion of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses is a valid, deferrable interpretation of the career-offender guideline or an impermissible expansion beyond the guideline's unambiguous text. The split directly affects whether defendants with prior drug conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under substantially enhanced sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is entitled to controlling weight as the Commission's authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline, and inchoate offenses qualify as predicate controlled substance offenses.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses from the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' and the commentary impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its plain meaning.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is sufficient to disqualify them. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for similarly situated defendants depending on where they are prosecuted, directly affecting mandatory minimum sentences.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are met.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the First Step Act's non-retroactive anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) allowing such claims exceeds the Commission's authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's elimination of stacked § 924(c) mandatory minimums, can support compassionate release. Some circuits hold that non-retroactive changes in law can never be extraordinary and compelling reasons, while the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to its policy statement attempts to permit such claims. This affects thousands of prisoners serving stacked 25-year mandatory minimum sentences.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state-controlled substance is not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects whether prior state convictions for substances not on the federal schedules can trigger enhanced base offense levels or career-offender status.

positions.label: State-controlled substance suffices
positions.summary: Holds that there is no textual basis to graft a federal-law limitation onto the career-offender guideline, and an offense under state law involving a state-controlled substance qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense.'

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they may bring claims through civil rights statutes such as Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoner challenges that affect the execution of a sentence but do not directly challenge the fact or duration of confinement, such as challenges to BOP decisions on prerelease custody or earned time credits under the First Step Act. The Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez and has not resolved it since.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus under § 2241 is available when prisoners challenge conditions or terms of confinement that affect the execution of their sentence, including BOP decisions on prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is limited to fact/duration challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and challenges to conditions of confinement must be brought through civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal deadline for filing a notice of appeal applies to an order resolving a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, noting a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case and the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that appreciation belongs to the estate based on the broad scope of § 541(a), while other circuits have taken the opposite view. This split has significant practical consequences for debtors who convert in good faith after their property increases in value.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A), read together with § 541(a)'s broad definition of estate property, post-petition pre-conversion appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, purpose, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be oriented toward facilitating reentry and protecting the public.
splits.description: Circuits are split on the permissible purposes of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for supervised release violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences should focus on the defendant's breach of trust and reintegration rather than punishment for the underlying violation.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, consistent with the court's broad sentencing discretion.

positions.label: Punishment is impermissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be oriented toward the defendant's breach of trust, reentry needs, and public protection rather than punishment for the supervised release violation itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be fixed as of the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year) or whether the actuary may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for the thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be determined by the statutory measurement date, providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond what was specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authority.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock does not run during the period of absconding, extending the court's jurisdiction to revoke supervised release.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling the term of supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and judicial creation of such a doctrine impermissibly extends punishment beyond the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits claims that were raised in a prior application — when filing successive § 2255 motions, or whether they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law. Applying (b)(1) imposes a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended for federal prisoners.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, in addition to the requirements of § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, and such prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s independent requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election rules such as mail-in ballot counting deadlines. The resolution of this question affects whether election-administration disputes can be adjudicated before elections occur or are funneled into post-election litigation, with significant implications for voting procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office suffers a cognizable competitive injury from laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes, giving the candidate Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized interest in fair elections is insufficient to establish Article III standing for pre-election challenges to ballot-counting procedures.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order involving a value of 'high order' that is effectively unreviewable after final judgment.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review of an order denying a motion to seal, creating potential tension with circuits that have taken a narrower view of the collateral order doctrine for sealing orders. This affects litigants' ability to protect sensitive medical information disclosed in litigation before final judgment.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders, including those involving medical information, do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements for immediate appeal and must await final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve questions about legal standards for business establishment discrimination claims, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently unsettled or in conflict with other circuits to warrant review. The decision could impact hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: The Second Circuit applied standards for discrimination or unfair treatment claims in hospitality that SCOTUS found warranted review, suggesting a potential conflict with other circuits.

positions.label: Alternative approach
positions.summary: Other circuits may apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the conflict that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
